key_concepts.concept: Score state changes acceptable tactical risk.
key_concepts.application: At deuce, break point, game point, set point, and tie-break mini-swings, the player should choose patterns that match their highest-reliability scoring route rather than chasing novelty.

key_concepts.concept: Singles is heavily shaped by the serve, return, and next two balls.
key_concepts.application: Backend tactics should separate serve plus-one and return plus-one records from generic rally records.

key_concepts.concept: The plus-one is a planned second ball, not an improvised stroke.
key_concepts.application: Serve location, return target, recovery, and expected next contact should be stored as one tactical unit.

key_concepts.concept: Rally tolerance is the base layer for tactical freedom.
key_concepts.application: Players who cannot sustain crosscourt depth should not be assigned high-frequency direction changes or low-margin attacks.

key_concepts.concept: Direction, depth, height, spin, and speed are the tactical controls of every shot.
key_concepts.application: Skill and tactic records should store which control is primary for the situation.

key_concepts.concept: Shot choice depends on whether the player is offensive, neutral, or defensive.
key_concepts.application: The same ball location can call for different targets depending on balance, court position, opponent position, and contact height.

key_concepts.concept: Crosscourt patterns usually provide more court length and recovery time than early down-the-line changes.
key_concepts.application: The down-the-line change should be gated by contact quality, balance, ball height, and opponent court position.

key_concepts.concept: Depth protects neutral and defensive states.
key_concepts.application: A high, deep ball is a valid tactical reset when under pressure, especially on slower or higher-bouncing surfaces.

key_concepts.concept: Spin can create net clearance, control depth, change bounce, and buy recovery time.
key_concepts.application: Topspin-heavy patterns should be paired with shoulder, trunk, forearm, and fatigue monitoring.

key_concepts.concept: Short balls create an obligation to improve court position or end the opponent's time.
key_concepts.application: A short-ball attack record should include approach direction, recovery to volley position, and pass/lob expectation.

key_concepts.concept: Against a net player, the choice is not only winner attempt; pass, body ball, dipper, and lob are all pressure tools.
key_concepts.application: Passing/lob records should store opponent net distance, player balance, contact height, and available court.

key_concepts.concept: Surface modifies bounce, movement, point length, and the value of first-strike tennis.
key_concepts.application: Clay, hard, and grass should alter tactical emphasis, movement dose, and load flags.

key_concepts.concept: Heat, wind, sun, humidity, and cold alter both tactics and physical tolerance.
key_concepts.application: Competition-day plans should adjust target size, rally length expectations, hydration breaks, and serve intent.

key_concepts.concept: Lefty-righty matchups create unusual serve and rally angles for many players.
key_concepts.application: Practice plans should include exposure to lefty patterns or lefty-simulated targets before relevant matches.

key_concepts.concept: Advanced tactics are opponent-specific constraints, not generic preferences.
key_concepts.application: The plan should rank opponent weakness, movement pattern, preferred contact height, second-serve vulnerability, and pressure response.

key_concepts.concept: Competition week should sharpen existing tactical patterns rather than add new high-complexity choices.
key_concepts.application: The backend should reduce novelty and load while preserving serve-return, plus-one, and pressure-point rehearsals.

technical_models.name: Five Ball Controls
technical_models.model: Every tactical shot can be described by direction, depth, height, spin, and speed. One or two controls should dominate the coaching cue for a given drill.

technical_models.name: Serve Plus-One Map
technical_models.model: Serve location predicts common return corridors; the server prepares the next ball based on likely return height, direction, and depth.

technical_models.name: Return Plus-One Map
technical_models.model: Return quality is judged by whether it neutralizes or pressures the server's plus-one, then prepares the receiver's next court position.

technical_models.name: Offensive-Neutral-Defensive Classifier
technical_models.model: Classify the player state from balance, time, contact height, court position, opponent position, and ball quality before selecting target risk.

technical_models.name: Crosscourt Tolerance Ladder
technical_models.model: Progress from cooperative crosscourt depth, to neutral pressure, to height/spin variation, to direction change only after stable contact and recovery.

technical_models.name: Down-The-Line Gate
technical_models.model: Change direction down the line when the player is balanced, contact is in front, the ball is not too low or too stretched, and the opponent is exposed.

technical_models.name: Depth-Height Reset
technical_models.model: When defensive, prioritize net clearance, depth, and recovery time over pace or line targets.

technical_models.name: Short-Ball Attack
technical_models.model: Short-ball decisions are built from ball height, player movement direction, opponent position, and whether the attack should finish, approach, or force a weak pass.

technical_models.name: Pass-Lob Selection
technical_models.model: Select dip, pass, body ball, or lob based on net player's closing distance, reach, court coverage, and the hitter's contact height.

technical_models.name: Opponent Scouting Grid
technical_models.model: Build a match plan from serve patterns, return depth, wing tolerance, preferred rally length, movement weakness, pressure response, and surface comfort.

technical_models.name: Lefty-Righty Angle Map
technical_models.model: Lefty serve and rally patterns should be rehearsed as angle-specific constraints, especially wide serves and crosscourt forehand/backhand exchanges.

technical_models.name: Score-State Tactical Menu
technical_models.model: Preselect a small number of reliable patterns for 0-30, 30-30, deuce, break point, game point, and tie-break score states.

technical_models.name: Surface and Weather Modifier
technical_models.model: Modify targets, rally length tolerance, approach frequency, movement plan, and load by court surface and weather.

tactical_rules.rule: Step inside only if contact quality and timing remain stable; otherwise use a deeper neutral return that denies the server's first aggressive plus-one.
Use a high-percentage body or heavy target when the line serve has become low percentage; the goal is a predictable return and playable plus-one.
Recover expecting a crosscourt or middle return, then attack the open court only if balance and spacing allow; otherwise build with heavy depth.

tactical_rules.situation: Serve plus-one after T or body serve
tactical_rules.rule: Expect a shorter or central return more often than a clean angled return, then use the plus-one to take time or change court geometry.
If the return does not expose open court, direct the plus-one to the opponent's lower-tolerance wing with depth before attempting a winner.
Deep middle is a valid neutralizing target because it reduces angle and asks the server to create width from a less comfortable plus-one.
Use crosscourt or deep-middle return targets before down-the-line attempts unless scouting identifies a major weakness and the ball is readable.

tactical_rules.situation: Receiver makes a solid neutral return
tactical_rules.rule: Do not over-recover blindly; hold a position that covers the server's likely plus-one from the return target.
Stay crosscourt with depth and shape until a short ball, weak contact, opponent imbalance, or clear open-court gap appears.
Use heavier height and spin to push the opponent back, then change direction only after creating space or a high contact advantage.
Only change down the line when there is a recovery plan for the opponent's crosscourt reply; line changes expose the diagonal counter.
Avoid aggressive down-the-line redirection from low, late, or stretched contact; lift crosscourt or deep middle to reset.
Create depth before angle when the opponent is balanced; angle without depth can give the opponent time and court.
Increase height and spin to buy recovery time rather than hitting flat pace from a compromised base.
Add pace only when contact is in the strike zone and court position is stable; otherwise prioritize spin, height, and depth.
When inside the baseline with high contact, reduce the opponent's time through earlier contact, flatter trajectory, or open-court target.
Build with repeatable depth, shape, and target discipline; the aim is to earn a shorter ball rather than force a low-percentage finish.
Use height, depth, and central targets to recover court position before trying to counterattack.
Set rally-length goals before tactical variety; a player who cannot make a target number of quality neutral balls should simplify pattern options.
High short balls can be driven or angled; low short balls usually need spin, slice, depth, or approach placement instead of raw power.
Approach to the side that limits the opponent's best pass or targets the weaker wing; avoid opening the opponent's favorite angle.

tactical_rules.situation: Player receives a short or central forehand
tactical_rules.rule: Inside-out is high value when it targets a weaker backhand and preserves recovery; inside-in requires a stronger balance and recovery read.
When the passer is balanced but the lane is covered, use a low dipping ball to force a difficult first volley rather than forcing a line winner.
Use topspin or defensive lob when the opponent closes hard and the passer has contact height or enough time to lift safely.
Aim at the body or feet when stretched and low; this can reduce the volleyer's options with less sideline risk.
Track serve location by score and side; pressure patterns often matter more than overall serve percentage.
Record return position and return target because these determine whether wide, body, or T serves create useful plus-one balls.
Identify whether the opponent dislikes high shoulder balls, low skidding balls, or pace; then choose height, spin, and slice accordingly.
Separate lateral weakness from forward-backward weakness; short-ball plans are useful only if the opponent struggles moving forward or passing.
Prepare for the lefty's ad-court wide serve angle and rehearse return targets that prevent the server's forehand plus-one.
Expect crosscourt forehand-to-backhand patterns to reverse normal comfort zones; pre-plan when to hold, redirect, or use height.
Increase rally tolerance, height, and depth while still protecting serve-return patterns; clay should not remove first-strike planning.
Prioritize serve accuracy, return compactness, lower contact preparation, and first volley/plus-one decisions because rallies are often compressed.
Blend first-strike patterns with sustainable movement; monitor repeated braking and recovery because hard courts can raise impact load.
Increase target margin, height discipline, footwork adjustment, and spin control; avoid low-margin line changes unless balance and ball read are clear.
Use high-percentage first-strike patterns and between-point routines to reduce avoidable long-rally tax without forcing reckless winners.
Shift serve target and toss management toward reliable locations; tactical intent should not require a serve action the player cannot repeat in glare.
Use one preselected serve plus-one pattern that the player trusts, then accept a neutral rally rather than double-fault or forcing a low-percentage first ball.
Make the server play a second decision: prioritize return depth or body pressure over winner attempts unless the serve is clearly attackable.
Close with a pattern that starts the point on the player's best serve-return advantage; avoid introducing a target not used earlier in the game.
Protect the lead with repeatable serve/return patterns and deep rally targets; do not donate the next point with unnecessary directional risk.
Return target should deny the server's favorite plus-one first; an early tie-break miss on a speculative return has high strategic cost.
Sharpen two to four established serve-return and rally patterns; do not install new tactical families when match freshness and confidence matter.
Use short pressure sets, tie-break starts, and break-point rehearsals to test decision quality without excessive volume.
Teach one target pattern at a time, usually crosscourt or deep middle, with modified balls or courts as needed.
Progress to two-pattern choice: hold crosscourt or attack short ball, then add controlled down-the-line decisions after consistency stabilizes.
Build match plans around opponent-specific pressure routes and test them with score constraints and surface-specific movement.

physical_demands.demand: Serve plus-one requires immediate landing recovery, split timing, and explosive first step.
physical_demands.tactical_link: A serve pattern fails if the server cannot recover into the expected plus-one court position.

physical_demands.demand: Return plus-one requires fast perception, compact swing adaptation, and rapid recovery from a short preparation window.
physical_demands.tactical_link: Grass, fast hard courts, and big servers increase the cost of long return swings.

physical_demands.demand: Crosscourt tolerance depends on repeated lateral loading, trunk rotation, and recovery footwork over many neutral contacts.
physical_demands.tactical_link: Rally-tolerance drills should track ball quality and movement quality, not only number of balls made.

physical_demands.demand: Down-the-line changes and open-court attacks require braking, re-acceleration, and recovery to cover the diagonal counter.
physical_demands.tactical_link: Directional tactics should be paired with deceleration capacity.

physical_demands.demand: Defensive phase requires wide-ball deceleration, sliding or lunging depending on surface, and enough aerobic recovery to repeat efforts.
physical_demands.tactical_link: A defensive reset is only useful if the player can recover before the next shot.

physical_demands.demand: Short-ball attack requires forward acceleration, controlled hitting while moving, braking near contact, and possible net transition.
physical_demands.tactical_link: Attacking short balls increases forward-backward load and should be practiced with recovery after the attack.

physical_demands.demand: Passing and lob sequences load shoulder, trunk, backpedal movement, overhead preparation, and recovery reactions.
physical_demands.tactical_link: Lob-heavy plans should account for opponent overhead and the player's own shoulder/back response if forced to defend lobs.

physical_demands.demand: Clay increases sliding and longer movement exchanges; grass compresses reaction time and lower-bounce setup; hard courts increase repeated braking impact.
physical_demands.tactical_link: Surface changes should alter movement preparation and tactical drill density.

physical_demands.demand: Pressure points require repeatable routines, breathing control, and decision simplicity under increased arousal.
physical_demands.tactical_link: The physical routine supports tactical execution by stabilizing timing before serve or return.

physical_demands.demand: Heat and humidity increase fatigue cost and can reduce movement quality, decision clarity, and serve/return precision.
physical_demands.tactical_link: Hot-weather tactics should include between-point pacing and lower-error patterns.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: High-intent serve volume increases shoulder, elbow, trunk, and lumbar load.
injury_or_load_risks.tactical_trigger: Repeated serve plus-one sessions, tiebreak serving rehearsals, or extra serve buckets after matches.
injury_or_load_risks.planning_flag: Track high-intent serve count and next-day shoulder, elbow, and back response.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: High return volumes against pace can increase wrist, forearm, elbow, and shoulder demand.
injury_or_load_risks.tactical_trigger: Return-plus-one blocks against heavy serves or machine-fed high-speed returns.
injury_or_load_risks.planning_flag: Cap high-speed return reps for players with wrist or elbow symptoms.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Large volumes of heavy topspin and high racket speed can increase upper-limb and trunk fatigue.
injury_or_load_risks.planning_flag: Balance spin-load sessions with recovery and technical efficiency checks.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Aggressive direction changes increase braking and recovery stress.
injury_or_load_risks.tactical_trigger: Down-the-line attack drills with live diagonal counters.
injury_or_load_risks.planning_flag: Monitor knee, ankle, hip, groin, and Achilles response after direction-change sessions.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Repeated short-ball attacks add forward sprint, braking, lunge, and net-transition load.
injury_or_load_risks.planning_flag: Count forward-transition reps and pair with calf, knee, and hip readiness.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Rapid increase in clay sliding exposure can stress adductors, hip, knee, ankle, and groin.
injury_or_load_risks.tactical_trigger: Clay defensive-reset and high-tolerance rally blocks.
injury_or_load_risks.planning_flag: Progress sliding exposure before heavy match simulation.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Hard-court sessions can accumulate braking and impact load in lower limbs and back.
injury_or_load_risks.tactical_trigger: Repeated wide-ball recovery, pressure tie-breaks, and long live sets.
injury_or_load_risks.planning_flag: Use session duration, change-of-direction density, and next-day lower-limb response.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Low-bounce surfaces can raise reaction and low-positioning demand, increasing slips or low-back/hamstring stress if unprepared.
injury_or_load_risks.tactical_trigger: Grass return and first-strike training without surface adaptation.
injury_or_load_risks.planning_flag: Build compact return, low-contact, and footing exposure before match intensity.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Pressure-point games can silently raise intensity even when volume looks low.
injury_or_load_risks.tactical_trigger: Repeated break-point, game-point, and tie-break sets.
injury_or_load_risks.planning_flag: Track high-arousal points and avoid stacking them after high serve or movement load.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Hot and humid conditions increase physiological strain and can reduce decision quality.
injury_or_load_risks.tactical_trigger: Long tactical sessions or matches in summer conditions.
injury_or_load_risks.planning_flag: Use hydration, rest, cooling, and conservative volume rules.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Adding new tactical patterns in competition week can raise cognitive load and disrupt confidence.
injury_or_load_risks.tactical_trigger: Late-week installation of new serve targets, return positions, or direction-change rules.
injury_or_load_risks.planning_flag: Restrict competition week to rehearsed patterns and small target adjustments.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Adult-style tactical volume can exceed junior physical and cognitive readiness.
injury_or_load_risks.tactical_trigger: Long full-court pattern blocks before rally tolerance and movement quality are stable.
injury_or_load_risks.planning_flag: Use modified-ball progressions, shorter constraints, and recovery checks.

training_implications.implication: Teach one reliable pattern before adding tactical branching.
training_implications.implementation: For beginners, use modified courts and balls to create crosscourt or deep-middle success before asking for down-the-line changes.

training_implications.implication: Tactical drills should include score constraints.
training_implications.implementation: Use 30-30 starts, break-point starts, and tie-break points so players connect decision quality to scoring pressure.

training_implications.implication: Serve and return should be trained as paired tactical systems.
training_implications.implementation: For every serve plus-one block, include a return-plus-one block that denies or exploits the same pattern.

training_implications.implication: Track plus-one outcome, not only first-serve percentage or return in-play rate.
training_implications.implementation: Record whether the first ball after serve or return produced offensive, neutral, or defensive state.

training_implications.implication: Rally tolerance should be measured by quality zones.
training_implications.implementation: Score rallies by depth, height, and recovery quality instead of raw rally count alone.
Only award down-the-line attempts when contact is balanced, in front, and above the minimum height threshold.

training_implications.implication: Surface-specific blocks should alter targets and movement dose.
training_implications.implementation: Clay blocks emphasize height, depth, patience, and sliding progression; grass blocks emphasize serve-return, low contact, and first-strike compactness.

training_implications.implication: Weather adaptation should be rehearsed before competition.
training_implications.implementation: Use wind-margin targets, sun-side serving adjustments, and heat pacing routines in practice rather than only discussing them before the match.

training_implications.implication: Players need deliberate exposure to lefty patterns.
training_implications.implementation: Include lefty serve simulations, reversed crosscourt lanes, and ad-court return patterns when a lefty opponent is likely.

training_implications.implication: Opponent scouting should be structured, not anecdotal.
training_implications.implementation: Create a pre-match form covering serve by side and score, second-serve target, return position, preferred wing, weak movement direction, and pressure pattern.

training_implications.implication: Short-ball attack training should include the next shot.
training_implications.implementation: After the short-ball attack, require players to recover to volley or passing coverage rather than ending the drill at the approach contact.

training_implications.implication: Pass and lob choices should be trained with live net-player reads.
training_implications.implementation: Randomize net-player distance and coverage so players learn body, feet, lane, and lob decisions.

training_implications.implication: Competition week should produce a short written pattern menu.
training_implications.implementation: List first serve pattern, second serve pattern, safe return pattern, pressure rally pattern, and emergency reset pattern.

training_implications.implication: Pressure can be trained without excessive volume.
training_implications.implementation: Use short sets, sudden-death deuce, and tie-break starts with clear rest rather than long fatigue-heavy play every session.

training_implications.implication: Tactical progression should be gated by level.
training_implications.implementation: Beginner: rally success and safe targets. Intermediate: serve/return reliability and two-pattern decisions. Advanced: opponent-specific and score-specific planning.

training_implications.implication: Every tactical drill should carry load-channel tags.
training_implications.implementation: Tag serve count, high-intent serve count, heavy topspin volume, wide-ball count, forward-transition count, and pressure-point intensity.

training_implications.implication: Tactical plans should adapt to pain flags.
training_implications.implementation: Elbow or shoulder symptoms reduce serve and high-spin volume; back symptoms reduce high-intent serving and extreme rotation; lower-limb symptoms reduce wide-ball and transition density.

training_implications.implication: Assessment should test decision quality under realistic constraints.
training_implications.implementation: Assess serve plus-one execution, return plus-one denial, crosscourt tolerance, direction-change timing, short-ball conversion, and pressure-point pattern adherence.

backend_records_to_create.purpose: Store reliable serve, return, and rally choices for high-leverage score states.
Model serve location, expected return, plus-one target, recovery, and load risk.
Model return target, depth, server plus-one denial, receiver recovery, and next-ball target.
Assess repeatable crosscourt depth, shape, and recovery before adding advanced direction changes.
Gate down-the-line changes by contact, balance, ball height, opponent gap, and recovery cost.
Standardize tactical tags for direction, depth, height, spin, and speed.
Classify point phase before recommending target risk.
Store short-ball attack choices by ball height, court position, opponent gap, and net follow-up.
Choose pass, body ball, dipper, or lob against a net player.
Capture opponent strengths, weaknesses, serve/return tendencies, movement issues, and pressure patterns.
Store handedness-specific serve, return, and rally adjustments.
Modify tactical patterns, movement dose, and load risk for clay, hard, and grass.
Adjust tactics and volume for heat, humidity, wind, sun, and cold.
Store tie-break serving, returning, mini-break, and pattern-protection logic.
Store server and returner decisions for break point.
Store reliable closing patterns that avoid late-game novelty.
Limit new tactics while rehearsing serve-return, plus-one, and pressure choices.
Progress tactical complexity from beginner to intermediate to advanced.
Map tactical drill types to serve, upper-limb, trunk, movement, and pressure load channels.
Modify tactical assignments when shoulder, elbow, wrist, back, hip, knee, ankle, calf, or Achilles symptoms are present.
Assess match IQ through plus-one, rally phase, direction-change, short-ball, pass/lob, and pressure scenarios.
